topic.shared.war-honor.title: War, honor, and collective cost
topic.shared.war-honor.body: Greek, Norse, Celtic, Egyptian, and Roman traditions all place power under pressure, but they frame honor, fate, kingship, and order differently.

cards.title: Same theme, different pressure
cards.body: Achilles’ injured honor, Ragnarök’s doomed fate, and Roman war-state identity all concern power, but each belongs to a different source tradition.

cards.title: Keep traditions distinct
cards.body: A shared theme is a question, not a blended canon. Compare the answers without merging the sources.

topic.shared.fate-return.title: Fate, death, and return
topic.shared.fate-return.body: Myths repeatedly ask whether fate can be escaped, survived, or transformed—and each tradition answers differently.

cards.title: Endings organize meaning
cards.body: Ragnarök, Osiris renewal, and Japanese underworld boundaries each place death inside a different cosmology.

cards.title: Return is not always rescue
cards.body: Some traditions emphasize restoration, others separation, and others transformation into a different form.

topic.shared.cunning-power.title: Cunning and dangerous intelligence
topic.shared.cunning-power.body: Odysseus, Loki, Baba Yaga, and Taliesin all show intelligence as survival power, but their moral positions differ sharply.

cards.title: Cunning crosses moral lines
cards.body: Cunning can preserve, deceive, test, or disrupt. The point is to track whose survival and whose order it serves.

cards.title: Speech becomes power
cards.body: False names, bargains, riddles, and poetic transformations all turn language into a survival tool.

topic.shared.otherworld-boundaries.title: Otherworlds and dangerous boundaries
topic.shared.otherworld-boundaries.body: The Egyptian dead, Celtic Otherworld, Japanese divine boundary, and Slavic water realm are not interchangeable places, but they all test the living.

cards.title: Crossing changes the rules
cards.body: Otherworld encounters make ordinary law unreliable: promises, gifts, tests, and appearances acquire new force.

cards.title: Boundaries create knowledge
cards.body: Death, water, enchantment, and sacred places reveal what the human world normally hides.

topic.shared.transformation-reception.title: Transformation and reception
topic.shared.transformation-reception.body: Stories change as they move between traditions and literary forms. Ovid’s Roman rewriting and the Mabinogion’s Welsh framing are different kinds of transformation.

cards.title: Reception is interpretation
cards.body: When one tradition reshapes another, the result is evidence about both the story and the culture doing the reshaping.

cards.title: Labels prevent flattening
cards.body: Calling Ovid Roman reception does not make him less valuable; it tells us what kind of evidence he provides.
